lessons.title: Factors Affecting Food Choice & Sensory Evaluation
lessons.description: Taste receptors, the olfactory system, sensory tasting panels, and the factors that influence food choices.
lessons.content_html:
How We Perceive Food: Taste and Smell

Every time you eat, several senses work simultaneously to build your impression of the food. Taste receptors are clustered in taste buds, most of which sit on the tiny bumps (papillae) on the surface of the tongue. These receptors detect five basic tastes: sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami (savoury). Each taste is a chemical signal — sugar molecules binding to sweet receptors, hydrogen ions from acids triggering sour receptors, glutamate compounds activating umami receptors.

Smell, however, carries more sensory information than taste alone. The olfactory system detects hundreds of volatile aroma compounds that drift up from food into the nasal passage — both directly through the nostrils (orthonasal) and retronasally when food is in the mouth. This is why food tastes flat when you have a blocked nose: the taste receptors still fire, but the olfactory contribution is lost. Together, taste and smell create what we experience as flavour.

Beyond taste and smell, two further senses shape our evaluation of food. Texture is detected by mechanoreceptors in the mouth — the crunch of a biscuit, the smoothness of a custard, the chewiness of a well-developed bread roll each come from different structural properties. Sound also plays a role: research shows that people perceive crisps as less fresh and stale when the sound of the crunch is dampened, even when the product has not changed. And appearance — colour, shape, portion size — sets expectations before any food reaches the mouth.

Key Fact

The five basic tastes are sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami. Combined with aroma (olfactory system), texture (mechanoreceptors), appearance and sound, these create the complete sensory experience of eating. Flavour is mostly smell — which is why a blocked nose dramatically reduces perceived taste.

Sensory Testing: Setting Up a Tasting Panel

Sensory testing is used in food development to collect objective data about how a product looks, smells, tastes, feels and sounds. Simply asking friends “do you like this?” is not sensory evaluation — it is an informal opinion. A properly set-up tasting panel uses controlled conditions: a neutral-smelling room, consistent lighting, palate-cleansing water between samples, and coded samples (e.g. labelled 376, 842, 519 rather than A, B, C) to avoid expectation bias.

The two main types of sensory test students need to know are preference tests and profiling tests. In a preference test, panellists are asked to choose which sample they prefer, or to rank several samples from most to least preferred. These are useful when a manufacturer wants to know whether a new lower-fat version of a product is as acceptable as the original.

A sensory profile test (or star diagram) asks panellists to score multiple attributes — sweetness, saltiness, sourness, crunchiness, aftertaste, colour, aroma — on a numerical scale (typically 1–5 or 0–9). The scores are plotted on a star diagram, giving a visual ‘fingerprint’ of the product. If a revised recipe is too salty, the star diagram will show a spike on the “saltiness” axis that can guide the next iteration of the recipe.

A very common mark-scheme error is to describe sensory evaluation as “I asked some friends if they liked it.” This loses marks because it describes informal opinion, not a controlled test. The key differences are: (1) a tasting panel uses a defined method (preference, ranking or profiling); (2) samples are coded to prevent bias; (3) the environment is controlled (no competing aromas, consistent lighting, palate-cleansing water); (4) results are recorded on a standard proforma so data can be compared. Without these controls, individual preference and expectation bias distort the results. For the 3- or 4-mark questions that ask you to describe how to set up a sensory test, include all four of these control factors for full marks.

The Range of Factors That Influence Food Choice

What ends up on a plate is the result of dozens of overlapping influences. The spec groups these into personal, practical, social and value-based factors — and your exam questions often ask you to apply several at once to a named individual.

Enjoyment and personal preference are the most immediate drivers. A 15-year-old who has grown up eating spicy food may find bland school-canteen meals unsatisfying. Past experience shapes taste: repeated exposure to a food in a positive context (a family meal, a celebration) builds preference over time.

Cost and availability are major practical constraints. A single parent managing a tight weekly food budget may rely on cheaper carbohydrate staples (bread, rice, pasta) and fewer fresh vegetables or oily fish, even when they know the nutritional value of the latter. Availability — what is stocked in local shops, what is in season — limits choice regardless of preference.

Seasonality shapes both availability and cost: asparagus is far cheaper in May than in December; Scottish raspberries are at their most flavourful in July. Eating seasonally can reduce food miles and support local farmers, but limits variety for consumers who want the same foods year-round.

Time and lifestyle are increasingly powerful factors. A working parent arriving home at 7 pm after a school run may reach for a ready meal rather than a slow-cooked stew, even if the nutritional comparison favours the latter. Convenience-food manufacturers explicitly target time-poor consumers.

Religious dietary rules can shape every meal. Muslim consumers follow Halal guidelines: pork and its derivatives are forbidden, and other meat must be slaughtered according to Islamic law. Jewish dietary law (Kosher) prohibits pork and shellfish and requires meat and dairy to be kept strictly separate. Many Hindus are vegetarian or avoid beef because of the cow’s sacred status. These are non-negotiable constraints, not preferences — a food manufacturer making a product for a multi-faith school canteen must account for all three sets of rules simultaneously.

Ethical beliefs shape choice in a different way. A consumer concerned about animal welfare may choose free-range eggs even though they cost more. A consumer concerned about climate change may reduce red meat consumption in response to the environmental evidence linking livestock farming to greenhouse gas emissions. These choices are personal convictions rather than religious obligations, but they are increasingly influential as food labelling makes origin, welfare standards and carbon footprint more visible.

Medical reasons and personal choices also restrict what some people can safely eat. A person with coeliac disease must avoid gluten entirely; a person with a peanut allergy must check every label for traces. These are physiological necessities. Personal choices — veganism, a low-sugar diet, a preference for organic produce — are voluntary but may be just as strongly held.

Food Labelling, Marketing and Informed Choice

Food labelling is a key tool for informed choice. UK law (Food Information to Consumers regulations) requires pre-packaged food to show: the name of the food, a list of ingredients (in descending order by weight), allergens highlighted in bold, net quantity, a best before or use-by date, storage conditions, and the name and address of the manufacturer. Allergen labelling is legally mandatory: the 14 major allergens must be emphasised in the ingredients list (typically in bold).

Front-of-pack traffic light labelling uses colour coding (green / amber / red) to indicate whether each nutrient (fat, saturated fat, sugar, salt) is at a low, medium or high level per portion. Research shows that shoppers use traffic lights to make faster decisions, particularly for fat and sugar, compared with reference intake percentage labels alone. However, critics note that traffic lights can mislead when portion sizes are unrealistically small.

Marketing also shapes choice. Bright packaging, celebrity endorsement, product placement at eye level on supermarket shelves, and advertising targeted at children all influence purchasing behaviour. The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) restricts adverts for high fat, salt or sugar (HFSS) products from being shown before 9 pm or on platforms primarily used by under-16s — acknowledging that young people are particularly susceptible to food marketing.

Key Fact

The full range of food-choice factors includes: enjoyment and preference; seasonality; cost and availability; time and lifestyle; celebration or occasion; culture and religion; ethical beliefs; and medical reasons (allergies, intolerances, health conditions). Exam questions often present a named individual (e.g. a Muslim teenager, a budget-conscious working parent) and ask you to apply at least three of these factors to their specific situation.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The 6-mark “Explain” extended response question rewards two or three well-developed reasons rather than six brief bullets. The command word “Explain” means “give reasons for and/or causes of” — you must use linking language such as “because”, “this means that” or “as a result” to connect cause and effect. A common mistake on sensory evaluation or food-choice questions is to write “it depends on personal preference” as if that is a complete answer. Preference is a factor, but an Explain answer needs to say why preference forms and how it interacts with other factors. For example: “A working parent may choose a ready meal over cooking from scratch because limited time after work means convenience outweighs nutritional considerations, even when they are aware that the ready meal contains more salt and saturated fat.” That single sentence earns two marks (reason + development) because it uses “because” and applies the reason to a specific scenario.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Flavour is built from five basic tastes (detected by taste receptors) combined with aroma (olfactory system), texture, appearance and sound. Smell contributes the majority of what we experience as flavour — hence why a cold makes food taste flat.
  • Sensory testing requires a controlled tasting panel with coded samples, palate-cleansing water and a standard recording method. Preference tests measure which product consumers prefer; profiling / star-diagram tests score multiple attributes to build a visual fingerprint of the product.
  • Food choice is shaped by enjoyment, cost, availability, seasonality, time, occasion, culture, religion, ethical beliefs and medical needs. Food labelling (allergen declarations, traffic light labels) and marketing both influence the decisions consumers make at the point of purchase.

practice_questions.text: Explain how food labelling and marketing together can help consumers make informed food choices, and how they can also mislead consumers. In your answer, refer to at least two specific labelling features or marketing techniques.
practice_questions.marks:
Use StudyVault rubric.

Mastering (5-6 marks): two or three well-developed reasoning chains covering both how labelling/marketing helps and how it can mislead; accurate technical vocabulary (allergen labelling, traffic light labels, HFSS advertising, portion size); applied to real consumer contexts; reasoning clearly linked with 'because', 'this means that' or 'as a result'.

Developing (2 marks): relevant points stated without reasoning chains; may cover only helping or only misleading; little technical vocabulary.

Content guidance: helping — traffic light labels (green/amber/red for fat, saturated fat, sugar, salt) allow shoppers to make faster comparisons; mandatory allergen labelling in bold protects people with life-threatening intolerances; best before and use-by dates reduce food poisoning risk; ingredient lists in descending order reveal actual sugar or fat content. lessons.title: Developing Recipes & Meals for Specific Needs
lessons.description: Adapting recipes for dietary and lifestyle needs — four development levers, time, cost and justified evaluation.
lessons.content_html:
What Does ‘Developing a Recipe’ Actually Mean?

Developing a recipe is more than swapping one ingredient for another. The spec is explicit that food development requires decisions about four things together: ingredients, processes, cooking methods and portion sizes. A student who answers “replace butter with low-fat spread” and stops there has changed only one ingredient — that is an incomplete adaptation. A thorough response considers all four levers: for example, replacing butter with olive oil (ingredient), switching from creaming to folding (process), changing from shallow-frying to grilling (cooking method), and reducing the serving portion to manage overall calorie intake (portion size).

This lesson brings together everything from the rest of the unit — nutrition knowledge, food science, dietary needs, sensory evaluation — and applies it to a practical brief. In your exam, extended-response questions at 8 or 12 marks often present a named person with a specific need and ask you to evaluate how well a set of adaptations would meet that need. The ability to justify and explain your choices, and to weigh strengths and weaknesses against each other, is what separates top-band answers from mid-band ones.

Key Fact

The four levers of recipe development are: ingredients (what goes in), processes (how ingredients are prepared and combined), cooking methods (how heat is applied), and portion sizes (how much is served). Exam answers that change only the ingredients are incomplete — always consider all four.

Adapting Recipes for Dietary Needs

The spec requires students to plan and adapt recipes for a range of specific dietary needs. The most commonly tested examples are:

Coeliac disease. People with coeliac disease have an autoimmune reaction to gluten, the protein in wheat, barley and rye. Even a small amount can damage the lining of the small intestine and impair nutrient absorption. Adapting a recipe for a coeliac person requires replacing all gluten-containing flour with alternatives such as rice flour, buckwheat flour or certified gluten-free oat flour. However, this is a process change too: gluten provides the stretchy network that traps gas and gives baked goods their structure. Gluten-free baking often needs xanthan gum (a stabiliser) or an extra egg to replicate this structural function, or the resulting cake will be crumbly and dense.

Type 2 diabetes. People with type 2 diabetes need to manage blood glucose levels by reducing free sugars and increasing dietary fibre (NSP), which slows glucose absorption. Recipe adaptation might include: replacing white flour with wholemeal (ingredient), using smaller portions of starchy foods (portion size), choosing steaming over roasting with oil (cooking method) to reduce the overall energy density, and using naturally sweet vegetables like butternut squash to reduce added sugar (ingredient). The aim is a lower glycaemic load overall, not just one ingredient swap.

Lactose intolerance. People who cannot digest lactose (the sugar in milk) need recipes that replace dairy milk, butter and cream with lactose-free alternatives: plant-based milks (oat, almond, soya), dairy-free spread or coconut cream. The sensory properties of the dish may change: oat milk has a sweeter flavour than cows’ milk; coconut cream adds richness but also a coconut aroma that may not be appropriate for a savoury dish.

Vegetarian and vegan diets. The spec distinguishes three vegetarian categories. Lacto-ovo vegetarians eat dairy and eggs but not meat or fish. Lacto vegetarians eat dairy but not eggs or meat. Vegans exclude all animal products. Adapting a beef lasagne for a lacto-ovo vegetarian requires replacing minced beef with a protein alternative such as Quorn, lentils or a combination — but the rest of the sauce and béchamel can remain unchanged. Adapting the same dish for a vegan requires also replacing the dairy milk in the béchamel and the Parmesan cheese on top. A key nutritional consideration for vegans is ensuring adequate vitamin B12, iron and calcium, which are less bioavailable from plant sources than animal sources.

A very common marking pitfall is to name one ingredient substitution and present it as a complete recipe adaptation. The spec and mark schemes expect students to consider all four levers (ingredients, processes, cooking methods, portion sizes). In a 12-mark Evaluate question about adapting a dish for a named individual, a top-band response will typically change at least two levers and explain why each change addresses the brief, what sensory or functional consequence that change has, and whether the benefit outweighs any drawback. For example: “Replacing plain white flour with wholemeal in the pastry case increases fibre content (ingredient), but wholemeal flour contains less gluten-forming protein, meaning the pastry will be crumblier and harder to roll thin (consequence). To compensate, a small amount of plain flour could be retained in a 50/50 blend (further adaptation), which preserves some workability while still increasing the NSP content compared to the original recipe (justified judgement).”

Managing Time, Cost and Lifestyle

Recipe development does not happen in isolation from real-world constraints. The spec specifically mentions working parents needing dishes that are quick to prepare and cook. When developing a recipe for this group, time management is a design criterion alongside nutrition. Techniques that save time include: batch cooking (making a large quantity and freezing in portions); preparing ingredients in advance (a mirepoix of onion, carrot and celery can be refrigerated for 3 days); choosing cooking methods with shorter active cooking time (a stir-fry takes 8 minutes from wok to plate; a slow stew needs 2 hours even if most of that is unattended).

Cost is a parallel constraint. A low-budget recipe adaptation might replace chicken breast (higher cost per kg) with chicken thighs (lower cost, more fat but more flavour), or substitute fresh herbs with dried to reduce waste. Per-portion costing — dividing the total ingredient cost by the number of servings — is a practical skill the spec expects students to use when justifying recipe decisions.

Testing, Evaluating and Improving Recipes

Once a recipe adaptation has been tried, it must be evaluated against the original brief. The process mirrors sensory evaluation (covered in Lesson 6): the adapted dish is tasted and assessed for appearance, aroma, flavour, texture and — where relevant — sound. Sensory descriptors should be precise: not “it tasted nice” but “the wholemeal pastry had a nutty, slightly bitter flavour and a coarser texture compared to the original.”

Adjusting seasoning is explicitly mentioned in the spec as part of the development cycle. Salt enhances and balances other flavours — a dish that tastes flat may need salt rather than more of another ingredient. Acid (lemon juice, vinegar) brightens flavour; sugar balances acidity. Learning to identify which flavour dimension is missing and adjusting accordingly is a core practical skill.

After testing, the developer produces a justified evaluation: a clear explanation of what changes were made, why they were made, how they meet the nutritional or lifestyle brief, and what further improvements could be made. In an exam question, “justify” means provide reasons that weigh the benefit of the change against any potential drawback.

The spec gives steaming instead of boiling as its example of choosing an appropriate technique for a specific outcome. This is worth remembering as a model for how the principle works. When broccoli is boiled, water-soluble vitamins (vitamin C, B vitamins) leach into the cooking water; if that water is discarded, up to 50% of the vitamin C can be lost. When the same broccoli is steamed, it is never submerged in water, so much less vitamin loss occurs — the sensory outcome (colour, slight bite) is also generally preferred. The same principle applies to other cooking-method swaps: grilling rather than shallow-frying reduces fat content; baking rather than deep-frying a potato changes the texture (soft interior but without added fat from frying). Every method swap must be justified by explaining what the benefit is and whether any sensory or structural trade-off results.

Key Fact

Choosing the right technique is part of recipe development. Steaming instead of boiling preserves water-soluble vitamins because the food is not submerged. Grilling instead of frying reduces total fat. Wholemeal instead of white flour increases NSP but can make pastry crumblier. For every technique swap in a development answer, state the benefit AND any sensory or structural consequence.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The 12-mark Evaluate question is the highest tariff question on the written paper. The command word “Evaluate” means “make a reasoned qualitative judgement, weighing strengths and weaknesses against a clear criterion.” The single most common reason students miss the top band is not reaching a supported judgement — they list adaptations and their effects but never say which approach is stronger or why. A top-band Evaluate answer on recipe development typically: (1) identifies at least three adaptations across two or more of the four levers (ingredients, processes, cooking methods, portion sizes); (2) explains the nutritional or lifestyle benefit of each adaptation using ‘because’ or ‘this means that’; (3) acknowledges at least one sensory or practical trade-off; and (4) reaches a supported final judgement — for example, “Overall, the most significant adaptation is switching from white to wholemeal flour because it addresses the brief’s NSP requirement directly and at low cost, despite the slightly coarser texture, which can be mitigated by using a 50/50 blend.” Without that judgement, the answer will be capped at Secure regardless of the quality of the content above it.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Recipe development requires decisions about four levers together: ingredients, processes, cooking methods and portion sizes. Changing only one ingredient is not a complete adaptation — extended-response answers must address at least two levers with reasoned justification.
  • Key dietary needs tested on the written paper include: coeliac disease (replace all gluten; add a structural binder), type 2 diabetes (reduce free sugars, increase NSP, lower glycaemic load), lactose intolerance (replace dairy; consider sensory impact of plant-based alternatives), and vegan/vegetarian diets (protein source, vitamin B12 and calcium implications).
  • Effective recipe evaluation states what was changed, why it meets the brief, what sensory or nutritional trade-off exists, and then reaches a supported final judgement. Without the judgement, a 12-mark Evaluate answer cannot reach the top band.

practice_questions.text: A school food technician is adapting a standard shortcrust pastry recipe for a student with coeliac disease. Explain why simply replacing wheat flour with a gluten-free alternative might not produce the same result, and what process change could help.

Acceptable answers: gluten provides the stretchy network that holds pastry together and gives it structure when baked (1); removing it means the pastry is likely to be crumbly and difficult to roll without tearing (1); adding xanthan gum (a stabiliser) to the gluten-free flour blend helps replicate the binding function of gluten (1); chilling the pastry dough before rolling (process change) reduces handling time, which also helps hold the structure because the fat is firmer (1); using an extra egg yolk increases the fat and emulsifier content, improving binding (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Nia is a 42-year-old working parent who arrives home at 7 pm after picking up her children. She wants to cook nutritionally balanced evening meals in under 30 minutes. Currently she relies on ready meals three evenings a week. Ingredients: pre-washed salad leaves or pre-cut stir-fry vegetables (1) save preparation time so more of the 30 minutes is spent cooking rather than chopping (1); tinned pulses such as chickpeas or lentils (1) require no soaking or long cooking, adding protein and NSP to a dish in under 5 minutes (1). Process: batch cooking a base sauce at the weekend (1) means a home-made tomato or curry sauce is available in the freezer and only needs reheating with fresh protein and vegetables (1). Technique: stir-frying in a hot wok (1) cooks lean protein and vegetables in under 10 minutes, producing a balanced meal with less fat than shallow-frying and with vegetables retaining more vitamins than boiling would allow (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text:
Theo, aged 16, has recently been diagnosed as lactose intolerant. His favourite family meal is a creamy chicken and mushroom pasta bake, made with double cream, butter and a Parmesan topping. His mother asks for help adapting the recipe so that Theo can still enjoy it.

Evaluate how well a set of dairy-free adaptations — replacing double cream with oat cream, butter with a dairy-free spread, and Parmesan with a vegan Italian-style hard cheese — would meet Theo’s dietary need and maintain the sensory quality of the original dish. In your answer, consider the nutritional impact, sensory consequences, and any further adaptations that might improve the result. Reach a supported judgement about the overall success of the recipe development.
practice_questions.marks:
Use StudyVault rubric.

Mastering (10-12 marks): comprehensive evaluation of all three adaptations across nutritional impact, sensory consequences and further improvements; accurate technical vocabulary (lactose, dairy-free alternatives, sensory descriptors, NSP, saturated fat); all three levers of the adaptation clearly connected to Theo's specific need; at least one further adaptation suggested with justification; a supported final judgement that weighs overall success rather than just listing changes.

Secure (7-9 marks): covers most of the three adaptations with development; nutritional and sensory consequences addressed for most changes; a judgement is present but may not fully weigh strengths against weaknesses.

Developing (4-6 marks): relevant points on adaptations but limited development; may cover nutritional or sensory but not both consistently; judgement present but weak or partially supported.

Emerging (1-3 marks): basic identification of changes with little explanation of why; no or very limited sensory or nutritional analysis; no supported judgement.

Content guidance: 
Nutritional: replacing double cream with oat cream removes lactose (benefit for Theo's intolerance); oat cream is lower in saturated fat than dairy double cream (additional nutritional benefit); butter replacement removes a further lactose source; vegan hard cheese typically has less protein and less calcium than Parmesan (nutritional trade-off worth noting). 
Sensory: oat cream has a thinner consistency and a slightly sweet, oat flavour compared to the rich, neutral creaminess of double cream — the sauce may be less thick and may have a perceptible different flavour; a process fix is to reduce the sauce for longer or add a cornflour slurry to improve viscosity; dairy-free spread behaves similarly to butter in a roux but may have a higher water content, making the sauce slightly thinner initially; vegan Italian-style hard cheese melts differently and may not form the same golden crust under the grill. 
Further adaptations: adding a cornflour slurry to thicken the oat cream sauce; using a stronger-flavoured vegan cheese or adding a small amount of nutritional yeast to increase umami/cheesy depth; marinating the chicken in lemon juice and herbs before cooking to compensate for the reduced fat-richness of the sauce. 
Judgement: overall, the three adaptations successfully remove the key lactose sources from the dish (strong because the substitute ingredients are widely available and affordable), but the sensory quality — particularly the richness and creaminess — is likely to be noticeably different without further process changes to thicken the sauce. The adaptation is a good starting point but is not yet a direct equivalent of the original; Theo may need time to adjust his expectations of the dish's texture.
